## Segment 2: 01:02.125 => 14:49.125
The presenter continues the demonstration of the service, explaining its functionality and features. The service is described as an ARM service with a resource called GeoCatalog. The presenter highlights features such as managed identity, private endpoints, and platform integrations. The demonstration includes a walkthrough of the Azure SDK Review slides and a live demonstration of the service's capabilities, focusing on the GeoCatalog resource and its properties, including the geocatalog URI as the airplane endpoint. The presenter also discusses the complexity on the data plane side and demonstrates the web interface accessed via the geocatalog URI. The discussion extends to the categories of APIs available, including STAC for spatial temporal data organization, Tyler for data visualization and statistics, ingestion management for data throughput, and SAS for reading storage blobs. The presenter attempts to map these features to the interface and begins explaining the stack part, which is a standard used by many organizations to expose collections of geospatial data. The presenter elaborates on the STAC standard, comparing it to an MP3 playlist, and explains its extension of the GeoJSON standard with timestamps and other domain-specific properties. The demonstration continues with the presenter showing how to interact with the API, including hitting the API endpoint to retrieve collections and items, and discussing the metadata associated with these collections. The presenter further explains the stack part, detailing how items are added or deleted, which triggers API calls. The Tyler part is introduced, focusing on visualizing geospatial data on a map. The presenter navigates through various interfaces, demonstrating the functionality and integration of different microservices. The discussion includes attempts to find collections with specific configurations, such as Sentinel 2 and NAEP, and explores the rendering configurations and data cubes. The presenter demonstrates the use of stack APIs for listing and filtering items in collections, including setting time sliders and filtering by properties like cloud coverage. The Tyler part is further explained, detailing how the service turns large geospatial data into HTTP streams based on user zoom levels, using an open source solution called T Tiler for dynamic tiling, which saves storage costs by generating tiles only when needed. The discussion continues with the explanation of the T-Tyler API, its implementation of the WMTS standard, and the customization options available for rendering geospatial assets. The presenter clarifies the standardization of the API schema and the role of T-Tyler in implementing the WebMatrix tile set standard routes.

Transcript
```
WEBVTT

01:01.170 --> 01:04.690
<Speaker 1>So yeah, we scheduled this new meeting.

01:14.480 --> 01:14.960
<Speaker 1>All right.

01:14.960 --> 01:22.800
<Speaker 1>we have these slides, but I can show you in action what the service done does.

01:22.800 --> 01:31.520
<Speaker 1>I think in my experience, this is a this has been a best way to get a grasp of what it does.

01:32.720 --> 01:37.600
<Speaker 1>So, yeah, our service is an ARM service.

01:38.320 --> 01:42.400
<Speaker 1>We have one resource, ARM resource called GeoCatalog.

01:45.040 --> 01:51.120
<Speaker 1>GeoCatalog is a very simple resource from a control plane side.

01:52.400 --> 02:02.800
<Speaker 1>Obviously, it does a lot of features like managed identity and the future like private endpoints and all sorts of platform integrations.

02:03.680 --> 02:07.280
<Speaker 1>But the complexity really is on the data plane side.

02:07.920 --> 02:16.560
<Speaker 1>So one of the properties here is the geocatalog URI, and that's the airplane endpoint, which is resource specific.

02:22.160 --> 02:30.880
<Speaker 1>Yeah, so when I hit this endpoint in a browser, it redirects me to this web interface.

02:32.000 --> 02:36.400
<Speaker 1>And yeah, this can explain what

02:37.040 --> 02:38.960
<Speaker 1>or the API does more than this.

02:50.750 --> 02:59.310
<Speaker 1>Yeah, from, I'll start with like the categories of APIs that we have here.

02:59.870 --> 03:04.990
<Speaker 1>So one category, it should be in my, the slides here.

03:08.030 --> 03:11.150
<Speaker 1>There is a stack, which is

03:11.680 --> 03:17.200
<Speaker 1>kind of how we're query and organize the spatial temporal data.

03:18.000 --> 03:24.880
<Speaker 1>There's Tyler, which is about how to visualize or run statistics on the data.

03:26.080 --> 03:40.480
<Speaker 1>There is ingestion management, which is kind of a, not formally an extension of Stack, but it's APIs that help you ingest

03:41.120 --> 03:49.120
<Speaker 1>data with higher throughput by setting up some ingestion pipelines.

03:50.080 --> 03:59.760
<Speaker 1>And SAS is to help customers read assets that are stored as storage blobs.

04:01.120 --> 04:10.000
<Speaker 1>So I will try, it's not very clear from the interface how this maps to these features, but I think

04:11.760 --> 04:17.600
<Speaker 1>Yeah, I'll try to go through them and so that you can understand the API side.

04:21.360 --> 04:24.080
<Speaker 1>All right, so I'll start with the stack part.

04:25.440 --> 04:28.560
<Speaker 1>So stack is a standard.

04:30.480 --> 04:38.320
<Speaker 1>It's used by many organizations and companies to for to

04:40.080 --> 04:44.480
<Speaker 1>expose collections of geospatial data.

04:44.960 --> 04:51.520
<Speaker 1>So you could think of it as an MP3 playlist back in the days, something like that.

04:52.720 --> 04:54.160
<Speaker 1>So it's a standard.

04:55.280 --> 04:59.120
<Speaker 1>It catalogs things in space as an is time.

05:01.080 --> 05:08.080
<Speaker 1>It's an extension of the popular GeoJSON standard.

05:09.760 --> 05:12.560
<Speaker 1>GeoJSON doesn't have timestamps.

05:12.560 --> 05:14.000
<Speaker 1>Stack has timestamps.

05:14.680 --> 05:24.800
<Speaker 1>And there are many other properties that are very specific to this domain.

05:28.640 --> 05:36.000
<Speaker 1>So I don't want to expand too much on Stack, but one big resource is a collection.

05:37.200 --> 05:38.880
<Speaker 1>So when I hit this API,

05:39.440 --> 05:40.640
<Speaker 1>Slash collection.

05:42.240 --> 05:45.120
<Speaker 1>It returns a list of collections.

05:46.000 --> 05:50.960
<Speaker 1>If I click here on a collection, then this is calling an API.

05:51.280 --> 05:53.680
<Speaker 1>It's calling several APIs.

05:56.160 --> 06:06.720
<Speaker 1>One of them here is like like for this is just like a gets collection which used to populate this kind of metadata.

06:08.320 --> 06:09.440
<Speaker 1>everything you see here.

06:12.400 --> 06:16.560
<Speaker 1>This is a child of a collection called an item.

06:17.920 --> 06:28.160
<Speaker 1>So in this blade we're listing the items and if I click add item here or if I delete an item that triggers the delete APIs.

06:29.120 --> 06:33.600
<Speaker 1>So yeah, that this is about the stack part of it.

06:34.640 --> 06:39.040
<Speaker 1>There's more to it, but I can expand on that later if we need to.

06:41.200 --> 06:55.600
<Speaker 1>The Tyler part is what happens when you try to visualize the geospatial data projected on a map.

06:56.760 --> 06:59.840
<Speaker 1>Let's see, let's find one that works.

07:12.000 --> 07:12.960
<Speaker 1>This doesn't have...

07:21.620 --> 07:23.300
<Speaker 1>Yeah, this is Brent's.

07:23.300 --> 07:24.740
<Speaker 1>I think I guess data cubes.

07:27.220 --> 07:29.140
<Speaker 1>I have never used data cubes.

07:31.460 --> 07:36.780
<Speaker 1>Okay, so what it does here and...

07:36.820 --> 07:44.100
<Speaker 3>If there is there use of just for the correctly showing the function, find a collection with bugs and show that one, please.

07:44.340 --> 07:44.820
<Speaker 1>Which one?

07:45.680 --> 07:47.080
<Speaker 3>Any collection with COGS.

07:47.080 --> 07:54.880
<Speaker 3>So I think we have Sentinel 2, some of Sentinel 2 or some NAEP.

07:55.400 --> 07:58.000
<Speaker 3>Yeah, okay, this Sentinel 2 collection would be a better one to show.

07:58.480 --> 07:59.120
<Speaker 1>This one?

08:00.160 --> 08:01.840
<Speaker 1>Yeah, this one I've tried earlier.

08:01.840 --> 08:03.840
<Speaker 1>It doesn't have a render config.

08:03.840 --> 08:04.760
<Speaker 1>Oh no.

08:05.600 --> 08:05.800
<Speaker 1>Yeah.

08:05.800 --> 08:09.480
<Speaker 2>If you go to collections, yeah, there might be one of the Sentinel ones that works.

08:10.240 --> 08:12.080
<Speaker 2>Or yeah, one of these NAEP ones should be good.

08:12.080 --> 08:13.440
<Speaker 3>Yeah, one of these NAEP ones.

08:15.040 --> 08:16.240
<Speaker 1>But this let's try this.

08:18.640 --> 08:20.000
<Speaker 3>OK, this one might might work.

08:20.400 --> 08:21.600
<Speaker 1>OK, this is better.

08:24.080 --> 08:32.480
<Speaker 1>OK, so this blade here is calling the stack APIs that I talked about earlier, like listing the items in the collection.

08:34.240 --> 08:40.240
<Speaker 1>It's also calling some stack APIs for filtering on the items I can set.

08:41.520 --> 08:47.200
<Speaker 1>like a time slider, start date and end dates, can be an open date as well, open start.

08:50.160 --> 08:54.160
<Speaker 1>Yeah, I can have other properties to filter on.

08:54.400 --> 08:57.280
<Speaker 1>Like one common one is the cloud coverage.

08:57.920 --> 09:04.320
<Speaker 1>I can choose to only display assets with clear images.

09:04.480 --> 09:10.800
<Speaker 1>So in that case, this list would only have things, let's say under 5% cloud coverage.

09:13.280 --> 09:19.600
<Speaker 1>Yeah, the Tyler part is what happens on the right side here.

09:21.600 --> 09:37.520
<Speaker 1>Underneath, our service turns these large geospatial data into HTTP streams just at the right size, at the right time.

09:38.880 --> 09:42.960
<Speaker 1>At the yeah, depending on the zoom level that the user is at.

09:44.400 --> 09:54.160
<Speaker 1>And this is based on an open source solution called T Tiler, which is a dynamic tiling service.

09:54.480 --> 10:03.600
<Speaker 1>So typically a tiling service has like some static images are very expensive to store.

10:04.720 --> 10:30.800
<Speaker 1>because they need to be at different dimensions, different zoom levels, but with dynamic tiling, your raw data is what you have to store, and then you only generate the tiles when you need to, and that saves an enormous amount of money for customers.

10:32.960 --> 10:35.760
<Speaker 1>So that's what the browser is doing.

10:36.000 --> 10:39.600
<Speaker 1>It's calling these Tyler APIs.

10:39.760 --> 10:43.760
<Speaker 1>They're prefixed by slash data in our spec.

10:44.960 --> 10:50.800
<Speaker 1>And yeah, so they look like this.

10:53.280 --> 10:55.680
<Speaker 1>So most of them are get calls.

10:56.960 --> 11:01.200
<Speaker 1>I assume that they're meant to be like cached.

11:03.600 --> 11:07.120
<Speaker 1>So that's why most of them are like get calls.

11:08.800 --> 11:16.400
<Speaker 1>A lot of them use only path parameters in the URIs.

11:18.600 --> 11:20.640
<Speaker 1>And this can be pretty complex.

11:20.640 --> 11:32.320
<Speaker 1>Like this explains which image bands to pick, what formula to use for colors, and which file formats.

11:33.760 --> 11:42.560
<Speaker 1>Yeah, this is a very complex API which we inherited from this TTyler API.

11:46.560 --> 11:54.320
<Speaker 2>So you can mention this TTyler as an open source definition.

11:55.120 --> 11:55.320
<Speaker 1>Yes.

11:56.080 --> 12:00.080
<Speaker 2>Is that something that is standardized?

12:03.600 --> 12:13.680
<Speaker 1>Some of it is kind of like some of the model responses and like the return types are standards.

12:14.280 --> 12:20.400
<Speaker 1>Others not really like what I've shown about the like the path parameters.

12:20.400 --> 12:22.600
<Speaker 1>That's not something that's standardized.

12:24.880 --> 12:26.160
<Speaker 1>So yeah.

12:26.800 --> 12:29.360
<Speaker 3>Sorry, let me jump in for a second.

12:31.040 --> 12:37.960
<Speaker 3>TTiler implements the WebMatrix tile set standard routes.

12:37.960 --> 12:47.600
<Speaker 3>So while TTiler, the library is open source, the REST APIs that it exposes for us are a standard.

12:48.080 --> 12:57.760
<Speaker 3>And what TTiler does have some customizations on top of the standard, but in terms of allowing the users to control how assets are rendered.

12:58.080 --> 13:05.520
<Speaker 3>So some of these geospatial assets are like photos, so you can think of them like RGB images.

13:05.520 --> 13:08.720
<Speaker 3>Some of them are hyperspectral images.

13:09.280 --> 13:15.680
<Speaker 3>And mapping that data to colors is really up to the user for how to do that.

13:15.960 --> 13:21.120
<Speaker 3>And so detailer exposes mechanisms for controlling how data is rendered.

13:21.680 --> 13:24.320
<Speaker 3>But the URLs that the browser is calling,

13:24.960 --> 13:27.920
<Speaker 3>are not defined by D Tyler.

13:28.080 --> 13:29.200
<Speaker 3>It is a standard.

13:30.880 --> 13:32.080
<Speaker 1>What is the standard?

13:32.400 --> 13:33.680
<Speaker 3>WMTS.

13:38.880 --> 13:39.080
<Speaker 3>Yeah.

13:43.440 --> 13:45.280
<Speaker 1>But it, okay.

13:48.320 --> 13:54.480
<Speaker 1>Yeah, if you can share like the, I mean, does it have like an API schema?

13:54.960 --> 13:55.680
<Speaker 3>They do.

13:57.120 --> 14:04.480
<Speaker 3>You have to read through a bunch of documents, but there is a, it's not a very nice like open API definition.

14:04.480 --> 14:08.920
<Speaker 3>It's a PDF document with a lot of definitions on these are the routes that you must implement.

14:08.920 --> 14:10.000
<Speaker 3>This is what they need to mean.

14:10.480 --> 14:14.320
<Speaker 3>And yeah, that's what TTyler implements.

14:14.400 --> 14:16.400
<Speaker 3>All this geospatial stuff goes back decades.

14:16.400 --> 14:17.600
<Speaker 3>So, you know, it's.

14:17.720 --> 14:23.920
<Speaker 1>Yeah, but this would be like a subset of the TTyler API, right?

14:26.960 --> 14:39.240
<Speaker 3>Yeah, I mean, I think for this meeting, what's important to know is T-Tyler implements the WMTS standard, and so therefore we also implement it because we use T-Tyler.

14:43.640 --> 14:43.960
<Speaker 1>Sounds good.

14:44.160 --> 14:45.240
<Speaker 2>Thanks for the clarification.

14:48.240 --> 14:50.400
<Speaker 1>So yeah, there's a lot about the Tyler.
```

The meeting continues with a focus on SDK development, particularly around collection management APIs. Participants discuss the creation, listing, checking existence, and deletion of collections, highlighting unique features like the custom API for deleting collections. The conversation delves into the async nature of the API and feedback regarding Azure Core for async APIs. The team discusses rendering options, tiling settings, and metadata for visualizing tiles on a map, aiming to improve API design by unifying listing operations and handling multi-part requests efficiently. The discussion also covers the structure of listing operations, the use of open API linters, and the need for customization to conform to existing specifications. The team explores ways to model APIs that return arrays as standardized listing responses and discusses manual tweaks for multi-part requests. The conversation includes a demo of the Azure Planetary Computer Pro SDK, showcasing strong typing and rendering capabilities, and addresses issues with image upload and serialization in the API.

The conversation remains centered on the management aspects of API ingestion without delving into specific design guidelines. A quick time check is made, noting 35 minutes remaining to review API views for all four languages, and deciding whether to continue discussing samples or move to other high-level topics. The discussion further explores the use of the pie stack library and JSON filters, expressing a preference for text filters and SQL to JSON conversion, and client customization options. ## Segment 27: 01:46:08.562 => 01:52:57.688
The meeting continues with a discussion on API response paging and naming conventions. The team considers whether paging is necessary for certain APIs, given the expected size of the responses, and explores the potential need for paging if responses grow larger over time. Feedback will be shared with the data plane team to address this in future API versions. Additionally, there is a discussion on naming conventions, with comments on the generic nature of some names and the need for specificity. The team also discusses the use of GeoJSON types, suggesting referencing existing types in Azure Core instead of creating new ones. The conversation includes considerations for maintainability and the possibility of reaching out to the TypeSpec team to maintain a collection of types. The team aims to avoid excessive customization and ensure long-term scalability. The discussion also covers the potential modifications to generated code and the extension of Java class files, ensuring that these changes do not block previous releases. The team explores how to map types to core types without generating new files, using package references from Azure Core and decorators in TypeSpec to specify Java types for models. The discussion further delves into the use of decorators in TypeSpec to reference Java types, avoiding the need to modify auto-generated code. The team considers evolving the alternate type decorator to allow defining fully qualified language-specific types, enhancing flexibility for language emitters. The conversation also touches on the Pystack library and its implications for type specification.

The team discusses the naming conventions for SDKs, particularly the use of namespaces and categorization in different languages like Java and .NET. The team aims to ensure that the SDK naming aligns with existing standards and practices, facilitating ease of use and integration for developers.

Problem.valueString: Using unions in OpenAPI 3 is straightforward, but OpenAPI tools require discriminated types for polymorphism. This can lead to complex and error-prone API specifications, especially when dealing with multiple geometries or features. Developers often struggle with maintaining type safety and clarity in API definitions when unions are involved.

RecommendedSolution.valueString: Adopt discriminated types for unions in OpenAPI specifications. This involves clearly defining type identifiers within the API schema to ensure type safety and clarity. BEFORE: `type: [string, number]` AFTER: `type: object, properties: {type: {enum: ['string', 'number']}}`. This approach improves maintainability and developer experience by providing clear type distinctions.

Problem.valueString: Managing a large number of APIs within a repository, especially when not all are owned or controlled by the team, presents challenges in consistency and integration. This can lead to fragmented API experiences and difficulty in maintaining a cohesive SDK.

RecommendedSolution.valueString: Implement a centralized API governance framework to ensure consistency across all APIs in the repository. This includes setting standards for API design, documentation, and versioning. Regular audits and integration tests can help maintain quality and coherence across the API ecosystem.

Problem.valueString: When initializing API clients, developers often use generic endpoints that do not account for resource-specific configurations. This can lead to issues where the client does not properly interact with the intended resource, causing errors or unexpected behavior. This pattern is problematic because it reduces the flexibility and specificity of API interactions, leading to poor developer experience and potential security vulnerabilities. Common scenarios include initializing clients for cloud services or databases without specifying resource-specific endpoints.

RecommendedSolution.valueString: To improve client initialization, use resource-specific endpoints that align with the intended API interactions. For example, instead of using a generic endpoint like 'https://api.example.com', specify 'https://api.example.com/resource'. This approach ensures that the client is configured to interact with the correct resource, enhancing security and functionality. Before: 'client = ApiClient(endpoint="https://api.example.com")'. After: 'client = ApiClient(endpoint="https://api.example.com/resource")'. This pattern should be applied when initializing clients for services with distinct resource configurations.

Problem.valueString: APIs often require developers to register searches and sort results, but inefficient patterns can lead to performance bottlenecks and complex code. A common issue is registering searches without considering optimal sorting mechanisms, which can result in slow query execution and difficult-to-maintain code. RecommendedSolution.valueString: To optimize search registration and sorting, use efficient query patterns that leverage API capabilities for sorting. Problem.valueString: APIs often return complex data types such as JSON, binary, or XML, which can be challenging to handle efficiently. Title.valueString: Designing Client SDKs for Multiple Services

Problem.valueString: When designing SDKs for APIs that interact with multiple services, developers often face the challenge of managing multiple clients and credentials. This can lead to confusion and increased complexity, especially when services have different route prefixes but share common authentication mechanisms. Developers may struggle with organizing operations across these services efficiently.

RecommendedSolution.valueString: To streamline SDK design for multiple services, consolidate clients into a single client with operation groups for each service. This approach reduces the need for multiple credential instances and simplifies endpoint management. Before: 'client1 = Service1Client(); client2 = Service2Client()'. After: 'client = UnifiedClient(); client.service1.operation(); client.service2.operation()'. This design enhances usability and reduces cognitive load by providing a unified interface for interacting with various services.

Problem.valueString: Developers often face challenges when integrating external libraries with SDKs, especially when dealing with complex data structures like geospatial data. RecommendedSolution.valueString: To improve SDK integration with external libraries, ensure that SDKs can natively accept data types from popular libraries, such as PyStack for geospatial data. Problem.valueString: Including all APIs in an SDK can lead to maintenance challenges and potential security risks. Apply this pattern when designing SDKs for services with sensitive operations.

segments.description: The meeting begins with participants discussing the presentation of review material. One participant is asked to drive the meeting, starting with an introduction to the service and champion scenarios. The meeting is scheduled to review API views, which were not available during the initial review.

The presenter continues the demonstration of the service, explaining its functionality and features. The service is described as an ARM service with a resource called GeoCatalog. The presenter highlights features such as managed identity, private endpoints, and platform integrations. The demonstration includes a walkthrough of the Azure SDK Review slides and a live demonstration of the service's capabilities, focusing on the GeoCatalog resource and its properties, including the geocatalog URI as the airplane endpoint. The presenter also discusses the complexity on the data plane side and demonstrates the web interface accessed via the geocatalog URI. The discussion extends to the categories of APIs available, including STAC for spatial temporal data organization, Tyler for data visualization and statistics, ingestion management for data throughput, and SAS for reading storage blobs. The presenter attempts to map these features to the interface and begins explaining the stack part, which is a standard used by many organizations to expose collections of geospatial data. The presenter elaborates on the STAC standard, comparing it to an MP3 playlist, and explains its extension of the GeoJSON standard with timestamps and other domain-specific properties. The demonstration continues with the presenter showing how to interact with the API, including hitting the API endpoint to retrieve collections and items, and discussing the metadata associated with these collections. The presenter further explains the stack part, detailing how items are added or deleted, which triggers API calls. The Tyler part is introduced, focusing on visualizing geospatial data on a map. The presenter navigates through various interfaces, demonstrating the functionality and integration of different microservices. The discussion includes attempts to find collections with specific configurations, such as Sentinel 2 and NAEP, and explores the rendering configurations and data cubes. The presenter demonstrates the use of stack APIs for listing and filtering items in collections, including setting time sliders and filtering by properties like cloud coverage. The Tyler part is further explained, detailing how the service turns large geospatial data into HTTP streams based on user zoom levels, using an open source solution called T Tiler for dynamic tiling, which saves storage costs by generating tiles only when needed. The discussion continues with the explanation of the T-Tyler API, its implementation of the WMTS standard, and the customization options available for rendering geospatial assets. The presenter clarifies the standardization of the API schema and the role of T-Tyler in implementing the WebMatrix tile set standard routes.

The segment continues with a detailed walkthrough of the ingestion management interface, focusing on the process of adding storage BLOB URLs and the functionality of ingestion tabs. The visual content includes a demonstration of the interface, showing how users can create and manage ingestion sources. The discussion also covers the overview of four microservices: STAC, Tiler, InMa, and SAS, highlighting their roles in satellite imagery interoperability, dynamic tiling, data ingestion, and data authorization. The segment further explores the Planetary Computer interface, showcasing collections and ingestion setup, and provides examples of how customer data can be stored in a storage account, including JSON definitions of collections. The service connects to storage accounts, copies metadata, and transforms assets like images into optimal formats for cloud services. The discussion also touches on the ingestion of spatial temporal data from raw satellite sensors, emphasizing the time-consuming nature of these processes. The segment concludes with a focus on triggering and monitoring ingestion runs, including the status of items processed, succeeded, and errors, and the use of managed identity for storage account access. The SAS service is discussed for downloading assets directly from storage accounts managed on behalf of customers, and the architecture diagram of the data plane is presented.

The segment transitions into a detailed discussion on API and data management, focusing on the use of SAS URIs for accessing storage accounts and the role of managed identities. The visual content includes a presentation of the data plane architecture diagram, illustrating how resources are hosted on behalf of customers. The discussion covers the generation of signed URIs for asset access, the process of revoking access, and the simplicity of the API calls involved. The segment also delves into the enumeration of main terms related to STAC, Tiler, and ingestion management entities, providing definitions and examples. The presentation includes a JSON API viewer, showcasing the structure and properties of collections and items, and explaining the GeoJSON format used for geospatial data. The discussion highlights the challenges faced in defining type specifications due to differences between open API versions, and the flexibility allowed in defining property names within the GeoJSON format.

The segment discusses challenges in using unions with OpenAPI 3, requiring discriminated types for polymorphism.
